claims.evidence: Directly stated with specific stereological counts at 12 months of age.

claims.claim: The volume of the STN was reduced in 12-month-old BACHD mice compared to WT mice.
claims.source: Both the total number of STN neurons (WT: 10,793 [9,070–11,545]; n = 7; BACHD: 7,307 [7,047–9,285]; n = 7; p = 0.0262) and the volume of the STN (WT: 0.087 [0.084–0.095] mm3; n = 7; BACHD: 0.078 [0.059–0.081] mm3; n = 7; p = 0.0111; Figure 11A,B) were reduced in 12-month-old BACHD versus WT mice.
claims.evidence: Directly stated with specific volume measurements at 12 months of age.

claims.claim: The density of STN neurons was not different in 12-month-old BACHD and WT mice.
claims.source: The density of STN neurons was not different in BACHD and WT mice (WT: 121,248 [107,180–126,139] neurons/mm3; n = 7; BACHD: 115,273 [90,377–135,765] neurons/mm3; n = 7; p = 0.8048; Figure 11A,B).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with specific density measurements at 12 months of age.

claims.claim: At 2 months of age, there was no difference in the total number of STN neurons between BACHD and WT mice.
claims.source: At 2-months-old, the total number of STN neurons (WT: 10,373 [9,341–14,414]; n = 7; BACHD: 10,638 [10,513–13,877]; n = 7; p = 0.7104; Figure 11C), the volume of the STN (WT: 0.098 [0.090–0.125] mm3; n = 7; BACHD: 0.085 [0.080–0.111] mm3; n = 7; p = 0.1649; Figure 11C) and STN neuronal density (106,880 [98,100–115,985] neurons/mm3; n = 7; BACHD: 124,844 [115,479–145,711] neurons/mm3; n = 7; p = 0.1282; Figure 11C) were not different in WT and BACHD mice.
claims.evidence: Directly stated with specific stereological counts at 2 months of age.

claims.claim: STN neuronal loss in BACHD mice represents progressive degeneration rather than an early developmental abnormality.
claims.source: At 2-months-old, the total number of STN neurons (WT: 10,373 [9,341–14,414]; n = 7; BACHD: 10,638 [10,513–13,877]; n = 7; p = 0.7104; Figure 11C), the volume of the STN (WT: 0.098 [0.090–0.125] mm3; n = 7; BACHD: 0.085 [0.080–0.111] mm3; n = 7; p = 0.1649; Figure 11C) and STN neuronal density (106,880 [98,100–115,985] neurons/mm3; n = 7; BACHD: 124,844 [115,479–145,711] neurons/mm3; n = 7; p = 0.1282; Figure 11C) were not different in WT and BACHD mice. Together, these data demonstrate that between the ages of 2 months and 12 months BACHD mice lose approximately one third of their STN neurons compared to WT littermates.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the comparison of normal neuron counts at 2 months and reduced counts at 12 months.

claims.claim: STN neurons from 6-month-old Q175 mice exhibited severely reduced rate of autonomous activity compared to WT.
claims.source: STN neurons from 6-month-old Q175 mice exhibited a severely reduced rate of autonomous activity (WT: 7.8 [1.9–14.7] Hz; n = 90; Q175: 0.0 [0.0–6.3] Hz; n = 90; p < 0.0001; Figure 12A,B), though the regularity of active neurons was unchanged (WT CV: 0.2 [0.1–0.6]; n = 77; Q175 CV: 0.4 [0.1–1.0]; n = 42; p = 0.1506; Figure 12A,B).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with specific measurements from Q175 knock-in mice.

claims.claim: There was a large decrease in the proportion of active neurons in the Q175 STN (47%) compared to WT (86%).
claims.source: Additionally, there was a large decrease in the proportion of active neurons in the Q175 STN (WT: 77/90 (86%); Q175: 42/90 (47%); p < 0.0001).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with specific proportions and statistical significance.

claims.claim: Glibenclamide rescued STN firing rate and regularity in Q175 mice.
claims.source: Inhibition of KATP channels with glibenclamide rescued both STN firing rate and regularity in Q175 and increased regularity only in WT (WT control frequency: 9.7 [5.4–13.5] Hz; WT glibenclamide frequency: 10.3 [7.4–15.4] Hz; n = 8; p = 0.1094; Q175 control frequency: 4.8 [3.5–6.2] Hz; Q175 glibenclamide frequency: 11.0 [9.3–13.6] Hz; n = 6; p = 0.0313; WT control CV: 0.19 [0.13–0.47]; WT glibenclamide CV: 0.11 [0.10–0.21]; n = 8; p = 0.0078; Q175 control CV: 0.45 [0.35–0.71]; Q175 glibenclamide CV: 0.15 [0.10–0.17]; n = 6; p = 0.03125; Figure 12C,D).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with specific measurements before and after glibenclamide application in Q175 mice.

claims.claim: D-AP5 pre-treatment rescued firing rate in Q175 STN neurons to WT-like levels.
claims.source: Similar to BACHD, Q175 STN neurons recovered to WT-like firing rate following >3 hr pretreatment with D-AP5 (Q175 control: 4.6 [0.0–11.4] Hz; n = 45; Q175 D-AP5 treated: 11.6 [0.0–18.7] Hz; n = 45; p = 0.0144; Figure 12E,F), although the regularity (Q175 control CV: 0.16 [0.10–0.66]; n = 15; Q175 D-AP5 treated CV: 0.14 [0.09–0.32]; n = 12; p = 0.2884; Figure 12E,F) and proportion of active neurons (Q175 control: 30/45 (67%); Q175 D-AP5 treated: 33/45 (73%); p = 0.6460; Figure 12E,F) were unaltered.
claims.evidence: Directly stated with specific measurements comparing untreated and D-AP5 treated Q175 slices.

claims.claim: The 12-month-old Q175 STN exhibited a median 26% reduction in the total number of STN neurons compared to WT.
claims.source: The 12-month-old Q175 STN (n = 7) exhibited a median 26% reduction in the total number of STN neurons with no effect on other parameters (WT: 8,661 [7,120–9,376] neurons; Q175: 6,420 [5,792–7,024] neurons; p = 0.0111; WT volume: 0.081 [0.074–0.087] mm3; Q175 volume: 0.079 [0.070–0.091] mm3; p = 0.6200; WT density: 109,477 [82,180–115,301] neurons/mm3; Q175 density: 88,968 [63,624–103,020] neurons/mm3; p = 0.2086; Figure 12G,H).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with specific stereological counts at 12 months in Q175 mice.

claims.claim: The STN exhibits similar dysfunction and neuronal loss in both the transgenic BACHD and Q175 KI mouse models of HD.
claims.source: Taken together, these data show that the STN exhibits similar dysfunction and neuronal loss in both the transgenic BACHD and Q175 KI mouse models of HD.
claims.evidence: Directly stated as a conclusion comparing findings across both models.

claims.claim: Dysfunction in the STN occurs early in the disease process, prior to the onset of major symptoms in HD mice.
claims.source: Furthermore, dysfunction was present in HD mice prior to the onset of major symptoms, implying that it occurs early in the disease process (Gray et al., 2008; Menalled et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with citations to literature describing symptom onset in these models.

claims.claim: STN neuronal loss occurred at 12 months of age in both BACHD and Q175 mice, a time point at which striatal neuronal loss is absent but psychomotor dysfunction is manifest.
claims.source: Cell death in the STN also preceded that in the striatum, as STN neuronal loss was observed at 12 months of age in both BACHD and Q175 mice, a time point at which striatal neuronal loss is absent but psychomotor dysfunction is manifest (Gray et al., 2008; Heikkinen et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2014; Mantovani et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with citations to literature describing striatal pathology and behavioral phenotypes.

claims.claim: Dysfunction within the STN contributes to the pathogenesis of HD.
claims.source: Together these findings argue that dysfunction within the STN contributes to the pathogenesis of HD.
claims.evidence: Directly stated as a conclusion based on the collective findings of the study.

claims.claim: Astrocytes play a pivotal role in HD.
claims.source: Astrocytes appear to play a pivotal role in HD. Expression of mutant huntingtin in astrocytes alone is sufficient to recapitulate neuronal and neurological abnormalities observed in HD and its models (Bradford et al., 2009; Faideau et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claims.claim: Impaired uptake of glutamate by astrocytes contributed to the relative prolongation of NMDAR-mediated EPSCs in BACHD STN neurons.
claims.source: In the STN, inhibition of GLT-1 (and GLAST) slowed individual NMDAR EPSCs in WT but not BACHD mice and eliminated the differences in their decay kinetics, arguing that impaired uptake of glutamate by astrocytes contributed to the relative prolongation of NMDAR-mediated EPSCs in BACHD STN neurons.
claims.evidence: Directly stated as an interpretation of the TFB-TBOA experiments.

claims.claim: The modest differences in glutamate uptake observed in BACHD STN neurons may not be sufficient to promote NMDAR-mediated dysfunction.
claims.source: Whether the modest differences in glutamate uptake that were observed here are sufficient to promote NMDAR-mediated dysfunction in HD STN neurons remains to be determined.
claims.evidence: Directly stated as an acknowledgment of uncertainty about the functional significance of the findings.

claims.claim: Train stimulation may have slowed glutamate uptake sufficiently to occlude the differences in uptake observed in BACHD and WT STN neurons during single stimulation.
claims.source: Slowing of astrocytic glutamate uptake has recently been shown to occur during increased presynaptic activity (Armbruster et al., 2016). Thus, train stimulation may have slowed glutamate uptake sufficiently to occlude/eliminate the differences in uptake that were observed in BACHD and WT STN neurons during single stimulation.
claims.evidence: Directly stated as a speculation based on cited literature about activity-dependent uptake slowing.

claims.claim: The relatively low level of glutamatergic transmission present ex vivo is sufficient to impair firing in HD models.
claims.source: If the relatively low level of glutamatergic transmission present ex vivo is sufficient to impair firing then this impairment is likely to be more severe in vivo where STN neurons are powerfully patterned by glutamatergic transmission arising from the cortex, thalamus, pedunculopontine nucleus and superior colliculus (reviewed by Bevan, 2017).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that firing is impaired ex vivo and the reasoning about in vivo conditions.

claims.claim: Non-synaptic sources of extracellular glutamate may contribute to excessive NMDAR activation in HD mice.
claims.source: Non-synaptic sources of extracellular glutamate, such as diffusion/release from astrocytes (Cavelier and Attwell, 2005; Lee et al., 2013) may also contribute to excessive NMDAR activation in HD mice.
claims.evidence: Directly stated as a possibility with citations to supporting literature.

claims.claim: NMDAR activation can elevate ROS through Ca2+- and nitric oxide-associated signaling pathways.
claims.source: NMDAR activation can elevate ROS through a variety of Ca2+- and nitric oxide-associated signaling pathways and their actions on mitochondria, NADPH oxidase and antioxidant expression (Dugan et al., 1995; Moncada and Bolaños, 2006; Brennan et al., 2009; Nakamura and Lipton, 2011; Valencia et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with multiple citations to supporting literature.

claims.claim: Mutant huntingtin causes transcriptional dysregulation leading to defective mitochondrial quality control.
claims.source: Although we saw no evidence of basal mitochondrial dysfunction that was not attributable to increased NMDAR function, there is considerable evidence that mutant huntingtin causes transcriptional dysregulation, which leads to defective mitochondrial quality control, an increase in the proportion of defective, ROS generating mitochondria and an increase in opening of the permeability transition pore (Milakovic and Johnson, 2005; Panov et al., 2002; Fernandes et al., 2007; Song et al., 2011; Chaturvedi et al., 2013; Johri et al., 2013; Martin et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with multiple citations to supporting literature.

claims.claim: Basal mitochondrial dysfunction could render HD STN neurons especially sensitive to NMDAR-mediated transmission and signaling.
claims.source: Thus, basal mitochondrial dysfunction could render HD STN neurons especially sensitive to NMDAR-mediated transmission and signaling.
claims.evidence: Directly stated as an inference based on the literature about mitochondrial dysfunction in HD.

claims.claim: H2O2 can act on KATP channels by decreasing their sensitivity to ATP, reducing the ratio of ATP to ADP, and/or modulating channel gating through a signaling pathway.
claims.source: H2O2 can act on KATP channels by decreasing their sensitivity to ATP (Ichinari et al., 1996), reducing the ratio of ATP to ADP (Krippeit-Drews et al., 1999), and/or modulating channel gating through a sGC-cGMP-PKG-ROS(H2O2)-ERK1/2-calmodulin-CaMKII signaling pathway (Zhang et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature describing mechanisms.

claims.claim: H2O2 is likely to directly modulate STN KATP channels in HD mice.
claims.source: H2O2 is likely to directly modulate STN KATP channels in HD mice because disrupted firing was also observed when STN neurons were recorded in the whole-cell configuration with patch pipettes containing exogenous ATP. Furthermore, H2O2 break down rapidly rescued activity, consistent with a direct action on KATP channels.
claims.evidence: Directly stated as an inference based on experimental observations with exogenous ATP and rapid catalase effects.

claims.claim: H2O2-dependent modulation of KATP channels has been extensively characterized in midbrain dopamine neurons.
claims.source: H2O2-dependent modulation of KATP channels has been extensively characterized in midbrain dopamine neurons where it powerfully suppresses cellular excitability and synaptic transmission (Avshalumov et al., 2005; Bao et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claims.claim: The activation of KATP channels in STN neurons may represent a form of homeostasis that suppresses firing when mitochondrial oxidant stress is high.
claims.source: The activation of KATP channels in STN neurons may represent a form of homeostasis that suppresses firing when mitochondrial oxidant stress is high, limiting the possibility of oxidant damage and bioenergetic failure (Ray et al., 2012; Sena and Chandel, 2012).
claims.evidence: Directly stated as an interpretation with citations to supporting literature.

claims.claim: Chronic oxidant stress in HD can lead to lipid and protein peroxidation and nuclear/mitochondrial DNA damage.
claims.source: In HD, chronic oxidant stress can lead to damage, such as lipid and protein peroxidation and nuclear/mitochondrial DNA damage, which profoundly impair cellular function and promote cell death (Perluigi et al., 2005; Browne and Beal, 2006; Acevedo-Torres et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claims.claim: The level of STN neuronal loss at 12 months in the BACHD and Q175 models was similar to that observed in HD patients.
claims.source: Furthermore, the level of neuronal loss at 12 months in the BACHD and Q175 models was similar to that observed in HD patients (Lange et al., 1976; Guo et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with citations to literature describing STN pathology in HD patients.

claims.claim: The absence of neuronal loss in the cortex and striatum in BACHD and Q175 models at 12 months suggests that STN dysfunction and degeneration may be particularly influential in the early disease process.
claims.source: The absence of neuronal loss in the cortex and striatum in the same models at an equivalent time point suggests that STN dysfunction and degeneration may be particularly influential in the early disease process.
claims.evidence: Directly stated as an inference based on the temporal pattern of pathology across brain regions.

claims.claim: The STN is critical for constraining cortico-striatal activity underlying action selection.
claims.source: As a key component of the hyperdirect and indirect pathways, the STN is critical for constraining cortico-striatal activity underlying action selection (Albin et al., 1989; Oldenburg and Sabatini, 2015).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claims.claim: In the classical model of basal ganglia function, degeneration of indirect pathway striatal projection neurons is proposed to underlie the symptoms of early stage HD.
claims.source: In the 'classical' model of basal ganglia function, degeneration of indirect pathway striatal projection neurons is proposed to underlie the symptoms of early stage HD (Albin et al., 1989).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with citation to the classical model.

claims.claim: STN dysfunction and neuronal loss precede cortico-striatal abnormalities in HD models.
claims.source: Here we show for the first time that STN dysfunction and neuronal loss precede cortico-striatal abnormalities in HD models.
claims.evidence: Directly stated as a novel finding of the study.

claims.claim: Dysfunction and degeneration of cortical and striatal neurons occurs in concert with profound changes in other elements of the basal ganglia.
claims.source: Thus, dysfunction and degeneration of cortical and striatal neurons occurs in concert with profound changes in other elements of the basal ganglia.
claims.evidence: Directly stated as a conclusion based on the findings.

claims.claim: Therapeutic strategies that target the STN may be useful for treating the psychomotor symptoms of early- to mid-stage HD.
claims.source: Therapeutic strategies that target the STN may therefore be useful not only for treating the psychomotor symptoms of early- to mid-stage HD but also for influencing dysfunction and degeneration throughout the cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical circuit.
claims.evidence: Directly stated as a therapeutic implication of the findings.

claims.claim: The STN is an element of cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical circuitry critical for action suppression.
claims.source: The subthalamic nucleus (STN) is an element of cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical circuitry critical for action suppression.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the abstract.

claims.claim: In Huntington's disease action suppression is impaired, resembling the effects of STN lesioning or inactivation.
claims.source: In Huntington's disease (HD) action suppression is impaired, resembling the effects of STN lesioning or inactivation.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the abstract.

claims.claim: At <2 and 6 months of age autonomous STN activity was impaired due to activation of KATP channels.
claims.source: At <2 and 6 months of age autonomous STN activity was impaired due to activation of KATP channels.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a summary finding.

claims.claim: STN neurons exhibited prolonged NMDA receptor-mediated synaptic currents, caused by a deficit in glutamate uptake.
claims.source: STN neurons exhibited prolonged NMDA receptor-mediated synaptic currents, caused by a deficit in glutamate uptake, and elevated mitochondrial oxidant stress, which was ameliorated by NMDA receptor antagonism.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a summary finding.

claims.claim: STN neurons exhibited elevated mitochondrial oxidant stress, which was ameliorated by NMDA receptor antagonism.
claims.source: STN neurons exhibited prolonged NMDA receptor-mediated synaptic currents, caused by a deficit in glutamate uptake, and elevated mitochondrial oxidant stress, which was ameliorated by NMDA receptor antagonism.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a summary finding.

claims.claim: STN activity was rescued by NMDA receptor antagonism or the break down of hydrogen peroxide.
claims.source: STN activity was rescued by NMDA receptor antagonism or the break down of hydrogen peroxide.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a summary finding.

claims.claim: At 12 months of age approximately 30% of STN neurons had been lost, as in HD.
claims.source: At 12 months of age approximately 30% of STN neurons had been lost, as in HD.
claims.evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a summary finding with reference to HD patients.

claims.claim: The basal ganglia are a network of subcortical brain nuclei that are critical for action selection and central to the expression of several psychomotor disorders.
claims.source: The basal ganglia are a network of subcortical brain nuclei that are critical for action selection and central to the expression of several psychomotor disorders (Albin et al., 1989; Wichmann and DeLong, 1996).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claims.claim: The direct pathway through the striatum promotes movement and rewarding behavior through inhibition of GABAergic basal ganglia output.
claims.source: The so-called direct pathway through the striatum promotes movement and 'rewarding' behavior through inhibition of GABAergic basal ganglia output (Chevalier and Deniau, 1990; Kravitz et al., 2010; Kravitz and Kreitzer, 2012).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claims.claim: The indirect pathway via the striatum, external globus pallidus and subthalamic nucleus and the hyperdirect pathway through the STN suppress movement and rewarding behavior through elevation of basal ganglia output.
claims.source: In contrast, the indirect pathway via the striatum, external globus pallidus and subthalamic nucleus (STN) and the hyperdirect pathway through the STN suppress the same processes through elevation of basal ganglia output (Maurice et al., 1999; Tachibana et al., 2008; Kravitz et al., 2010; Kravitz and Kreitzer, 2012).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claims.claim: Interruption of the indirect and hyperdirect pathways through lesion or inactivation of the STN is associated with elevated/involuntary movement, impulsivity and psychiatric disturbances.
claims.source: Indeed, interruption of the indirect and hyperdirect pathways through lesion or inactivation of the STN is associated with elevated/involuntary movement, impulsivity and psychiatric disturbances such as hypomania and hyper-sexuality (Crossman et al., 1988; Hamada and DeLong, 1992; Baunez and Robbins, 1997; Bickel et al., 2010; Jahanshahi et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claims.claim: Huntington's disease is an autosomal dominant, neurodegenerative disorder caused by an expansion of CAG repeats in the gene encoding huntingtin.
claims.source: Huntington's disease (HD) is an autosomal dominant, neurodegenerative disorder caused by an expansion of CAG repeats in the gene (HTT) encoding huntingtin (HTT), a protein involved in vesicle dynamics and intracellular transport (Huntington's Disease Collaborative Research Group, 1993; Saudou and Humbert, 2016).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claims.claim: Huntingtin is a protein involved in vesicle dynamics and intracellular transport.
claims.source: Huntington's disease (HD) is an autosomal dominant, neurodegenerative disorder caused by an expansion of CAG repeats in the gene (HTT) encoding huntingtin (HTT), a protein involved in vesicle dynamics and intracellular transport (Huntington's Disease Collaborative Research Group, 1993; Saudou and Humbert, 2016).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claims.claim: Early symptoms of HD include involuntary movement, compulsive behavior, paranoia, irritability and aggression.
claims.source: Early symptoms of HD include involuntary movement, compulsive behavior, paranoia, irritability and aggression (Anderson and Marder, 2001; Kirkwood et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claims.claim: HD symptoms have traditionally been linked to cortico-striatal degeneration.
claims.source: These symptoms have traditionally been linked to cortico-striatal degeneration, however a role for the STN is suggested by their similarity to those caused by STN inactivation or lesion.
claims.evidence: Directly stated as established knowledge.

claims.claim: The hypoactivity of the STN in HD models in vivo is consistent with STN dysfunction.
claims.source: The hypoactivity of the STN in HD models in vivo (Callahan and Abercrombie, 2015a, 2015b) and the susceptibility of the STN to degeneration in HD (Lange et al., 1976; Guo et al., 2012) are also consistent with STN dysfunction.
claims.evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claims.claim: The STN is susceptible to degeneration in HD.
claims.source: The hypoactivity of the STN in HD models in vivo (Callahan and Abercrombie, 2015a, 2015b) and the susceptibility of the STN to degeneration in HD (Lange et al., 1976; Guo et al., 2012) are also consistent with STN dysfunction.
claims.evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claims.claim: BACHD mice express full-length human HTT with 97 mixed CAA-CAG repeats in a bacterial artificial chromosome.
claims.source: For example, one line expresses full-length human HTT with 97 mixed CAA-CAG repeats in a bacterial artificial chromosome (BAC; Gray et al., 2008), whereas Q175 knock-in (KI) mice have an inserted chimeric human/mouse exon one with a human polyproline region and ~188 CAG repeats in the native Htt (Menalled et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with citation describing the model.

claims.claim: Q175 knock-in mice have an inserted chimeric human/mouse exon one with a human polyproline region and ~188 CAG repeats in the native Htt.
claims.source: For example, one line expresses full-length human HTT with 97 mixed CAA-CAG repeats in a bacterial artificial chromosome (BAC; Gray et al., 2008), whereas Q175 knock-in (KI) mice have an inserted chimeric human/mouse exon one with a human polyproline region and ~188 CAG repeats in the native Htt (Menalled et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with citation describing the model.

claims.claim: Increased mitochondrial oxidant stress exacerbated by abnormal NMDAR-mediated transmission and signaling has been reported in HD and its models.
claims.source: Increased mitochondrial oxidant stress exacerbated by abnormal NMDAR-mediated transmission and signaling has been reported in HD and its models (Fan and Raymond, 2007; Song et al., 2011; Johri et al., 2013; Parsons and Raymond, 2014; Martin et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claims.claim: Several reports suggest that glutamate uptake is impaired due to reduced expression of the glutamate transporter EAAT2 (GLT-1) and/or GLT-1 dysfunction.
claims.source: Several reports suggest that glutamate uptake is impaired due to reduced expression of the glutamate transporter EAAT2 (GLT-1) and/or GLT-1 dysfunction (Arzberger et al., 1997; Liévens et al., 2001; Behrens et al., 2002; Miller et al., 2008; Bradford et al., 2009; Faideau et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2010; Menalled et al., 2012; Dvorzhak et al., 2016; Jiang et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with multiple citations to supporting literature.

claims.claim: Some studies have found no evidence for deficient glutamate uptake in HD models.
claims.source: However, others have found no evidence for deficient glutamate uptake (Parsons et al., 2016), suggesting that abnormal NMDAR-mediated transmission is caused by increased expression of extrasynaptic receptors and/or aberrant coupling to signaling pathways (e.g., Parsons and Raymond, 2014).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claims.claim: The sensitivity of mitochondria to anomalous NMDAR signaling is likely to be further compounded by their intrinsically compromised status in HD.
claims.source: The sensitivity of mitochondria to anomalous NMDAR signaling is likely to be further compounded by their intrinsically compromised status in HD (Song et al., 2011; Johri et al., 2013; Martin et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claims.claim: HD models do not exhibit similar levels and spatiotemporal patterns of cortico-striatal neurodegeneration as seen in HD.
claims.source: Although HD models exhibit pathogenic processes seen in HD, they do not exhibit similar levels and spatiotemporal patterns of cortico-striatal neurodegeneration.
claims.evidence: Directly stated as a limitation of HD models.

claims.claim: Striatal neuronal loss in R6/2 mice occurs close to death.
claims.source: Striatal neuronal loss in aggressive Htt fragment models such as R6/2 mice does occur but only close to death (Stack et al., 2005), whereas full-length models exhibit minimal loss (Gray et al., 2008; Smith et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claims.claim: Full-length HD models exhibit minimal striatal neuronal loss.
claims.source: Striatal neuronal loss in aggressive Htt fragment models such as R6/2 mice does occur but only close to death (Stack et al., 2005), whereas full-length models exhibit minimal loss (Gray et al., 2008; Smith et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claims.claim: STN neurons exhibit intrinsic, autonomous firing, which contributes to their role as a driving force of neuronal activity in the basal ganglia.
claims.source: STN neurons exhibit intrinsic, autonomous firing, which contributes to their role as a driving force of neuronal activity in the basal ganglia (Bevan and Wilson, 1999; Beurrier et al., 2000; Do and Bean, 2003).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claims.claim: The lateral two-thirds of the STN receives input from the motor cortex.
claims.source: Recordings focused on the lateral two-thirds of the STN, which receives input from the motor cortex (Kita and Kita, 2012; Chu et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claims.claim: The distribution of firing frequency of WT neurons appears unimodal with a mode at ~6–8 Hz.
claims.source: The distribution of firing frequency of WT neurons appears unimodal with a mode at ~6–8 Hz (Figure 1C), whereas the distribution of BACHD neurons is relatively bimodal with modes at ~0–2 Hz and ~8–10 Hz (Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p = 0.0002; Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 1C showing the distribution.

claims.claim: The distribution of BACHD neurons is relatively bimodal with modes at ~0–2 Hz and ~8–10 Hz.
claims.source: The distribution of firing frequency of WT neurons appears unimodal with a mode at ~6–8 Hz (Figure 1C), whereas the distribution of BACHD neurons is relatively bimodal with modes at ~0–2 Hz and ~8–10 Hz (Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p = 0.0002; Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 1C and statistical test.

claims.claim: BACHD neurons consist of a phenotypic population with compromised autonomous firing, and a non-phenotypic population with relatively normal autonomous firing.
claims.source: This distribution suggests that BACHD neurons consist of a phenotypic population with compromised autonomous firing, and a non-phenotypic population with relatively normal autonomous firing.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the bimodal distribution of firing frequencies in BACHD neurons.

claims.claim: There was no correlation between NMDAR EPSC amplitude and decay time in WT or BACHD mice.

results.result: Autonomous activity of STN neurons is impaired in BACHD mice at both presymptomatic (1-2 months) and symptomatic (5-7 months) ages, with reduced frequency, regularity, and proportion of active neurons. The firing frequency distribution in BACHD neurons is bimodal, suggesting phenotypic and non-phenotypic populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 provide comprehensive electrophysiological data with appropriate sample sizes (n=126-145 per group), statistical tests, and significant p-values at both age points. The bimodal distribution (C88-C90) is supported by Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (p=0.0002) and provides mechanistic insight into population heterogeneity. All measurements are internally consistent and use appropriate non-invasive recording methods.

results.result: Individual NMDAR-mediated EPSCs are prolonged in BACHD STN neurons due to impaired glutamate uptake, but compound EPSCs during train stimulation show no difference between genotypes. There is no increase in extrasynaptic NMDAR expression/function in BACHD STN.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C7 demonstrate prolonged NMDAR EPSC decay in BACHD (p=0.0455) and differential TFB-TBOA effects between genotypes with adequate sample sizes (n=9-12). The lack of difference in compound EPSCs (C92-C93) is well-documented and appropriately interpreted. However, C42 acknowledges uncertainty about whether train stimulation occluded uptake differences, suggesting the mechanism requires further validation.

results.result: NMDAR antagonism with D-AP5 rescues autonomous firing in BACHD and Q175 STN neurons, demonstrating that NMDAR activation contributes to firing disruption. The rescue is partially mediated through reduction in KATP channel activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9 show robust rescue effects with D-AP5 pretreatment in BACHD mice (p<0.0001 for frequency and regularity) with adequate sample sizes (n=30 per group). Similar effects in Q175 mice (C33) strengthen the conclusion. The occlusion experiments (C94-C95) provide mechanistic insight linking NMDAR antagonism to KATP channels, though the partial occlusion suggests additional mechanisms may be involved.

results.result: STN neurons from BACHD mice exhibit elevated mitochondrial oxidant stress, which is ameliorated by NMDAR antagonism with D-AP5.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11 use appropriate two-photon imaging of MTS-roGFP with adequate sample sizes (n=23-24 for genotype comparison, n=13-17 for D-AP5 treatment) and significant p-values (p=0.0332 and p=0.0445). However, C11 notes the D-AP5 experiment was performed 15 months later with a different cohort, which could introduce batch effects. The link between NMDAR activation and oxidant stress is well-established in the literature (C45).

results.result: KATP channels are responsible for impaired autonomous activity in BACHD STN neurons. Inhibition of KATP channels with glibenclamide or gliclazide rescues firing rate and regularity in BACHD but not WT neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C15 provide strong pharmacological evidence with both glibenclamide (n=15 BACHD, n=8 WT) and gliclazide (n=6), showing consistent rescue effects (p<0.001). The use of gliclazide (C15, C97) addresses the potential confound of glibenclamide's effects on Epac2/Rap1 signaling (C96). Whole-cell recordings (C14) confirm hyperpolarizing effects consistent with KATP channel activation. The conclusion (C12) is well-supported by converging pharmacological evidence.

results.result: Increased NMDAR activation in WT STN neurons can induce a persistent KATP channel-mediated homeostatic reduction in autonomous activity, as demonstrated by NMDA pretreatment experiments and rescue with glibenclamide or by inhibiting glutathione peroxidase.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C17 show that NMDA pretreatment in WT mice recapitulates the BACHD phenotype with adequate sample sizes (n=75-87) and significant effects. Claims C23-C24 demonstrate that increasing oxidant stress with MCS reduces firing, which is rescued by glibenclamide (n=11), providing mechanistic support. These experiments establish causality and demonstrate that the pathway can be engaged in WT neurons, strengthening the overall model.

results.result: H2O2 underlies KATP channel activation in BACHD STN neurons. Catalase application rescues firing in BACHD neurons, and this effect occludes subsequent glibenclamide application, indicating H2O2 acts primarily through KATP channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C20 demonstrate robust rescue with catalase (n=11, p<0.01) and complete occlusion of glibenclamide effects, providing strong evidence for H2O2 as the primary mediator. Claim C22 shows greater catalase effects in BACHD vs WT (p<0.01), supporting disease-specific elevation of H2O2. The reverse experiment with glibenclamide first shows minimal additional catalase effect, confirming the pathway. Claim C49 provides additional mechanistic support from whole-cell recordings with exogenous ATP.

results.result: BACHD mice exhibit progressive loss of approximately 32% of STN neurons between 2 and 12 months of age, with reduced STN volume but unchanged neuronal density, indicating progressive degeneration rather than developmental abnormality.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C28 provide rigorous stereological data with adequate sample sizes (n=7 per group per age) and appropriate statistical comparisons. The normal neuron counts at 2 months (C28) followed by significant loss at 12 months (C25-C26, p<0.05) strongly support progressive degeneration (C29, C104). The unchanged density (C27) is consistent with proportional loss of neurons and volume. The methodology follows established stereological principles with Gundersen CE <0.1.

results.result: The Q175 knock-in mouse model exhibits similar STN dysfunction and neuronal loss as the BACHD model, including impaired autonomous activity rescued by KATP channel inhibition and NMDAR antagonism, and approximately 26% neuronal loss at 12 months.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C34 demonstrate that Q175 mice show similar phenotypes to BACHD with adequate sample sizes (n=45-90 for firing, n=7 for stereology) and significant effects. The consistency across two independent HD models (transgenic BACHD and knock-in Q175) with different genetic constructs (C77-C78) strongly supports that the findings represent core HD pathology rather than model-specific artifacts. Claim C35 appropriately summarizes this convergent evidence.

results.result: STN dysfunction occurs early in the disease process prior to major symptoms and precedes striatal pathology in HD models. STN neuronal loss at 12 months is similar to that in HD patients and occurs when striatal loss is absent but psychomotor dysfunction is present.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C37 are supported by appropriate citations to the literature describing symptom onset and striatal pathology timelines in these models. Claim C53 correctly cites human pathology data (Lange et al., 1976; Guo et al., 2012). The temporal precedence of STN dysfunction (C57) is supported by the data showing impairment at 1-2 months (C4) and the comparison with striatal pathology timelines from cited literature. However, the manuscript does not directly measure striatal pathology in the same animals, relying on literature comparisons.

results.result: Astrocytes play a pivotal role in HD, with expression of mutant huntingtin in astrocytes alone sufficient to recapitulate HD abnormalities, and astrocyte-specific rescue approaches ameliorating HD model abnormalities.
results.evaluation: Claims C39, C105-C106 are appropriately cited from the literature (Bradford et al., 2009; Faideau et al., 2010; Tong et al., 2014; Oliveira et al., 2016) and provide important context for interpreting the glutamate uptake findings. However, these are literature-based claims rather than findings from the current study, and the manuscript does not directly test astrocyte-specific contributions in the STN.

results.result: The functional significance of modest glutamate uptake differences in BACHD STN remains uncertain, and additional mechanisms including activity-dependent uptake slowing, non-synaptic glutamate sources, and in vivo glutamatergic drive may contribute to NMDAR dysfunction.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C44 appropriately acknowledge limitations and uncertainties in the data. Claim C41 explicitly states uncertainty about whether the observed uptake differences are sufficient for dysfunction. Claims C42 and C44 are speculative (marked as SPECULATION in evidence_type) and cite relevant literature but lack direct experimental support. Claim C43 is an inference about in vivo conditions based on ex vivo observations. These represent important caveats and future directions rather than established findings.

results.result: NMDAR activation can elevate ROS through multiple signaling pathways, and mutant huntingtin causes mitochondrial dysfunction that may render HD neurons especially sensitive to NMDAR-mediated stress. H2O2 can modulate KATP channels through multiple mechanisms, potentially representing a homeostatic response to oxidant stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C52 are well-supported by extensive literature citations and provide important mechanistic context for the findings. However, these are primarily literature-based knowledge claims rather than novel findings from the current study. Claim C47 is an inference about potential synergy between NMDAR activation and basal mitochondrial dysfunction, which is reasonable but not directly tested. The claims appropriately frame the study's findings within established mechanisms.

results.result: The STN is critical for action selection through the indirect and hyperdirect pathways. Classical models attribute HD symptoms to striatal degeneration, but therapeutic strategies targeting the STN may be useful for treating early- to mid-stage HD symptoms.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C56 are well-established knowledge appropriately cited from the literature. Claim C59 is a speculative therapeutic implication (marked as SPECULATION) that logically follows from the findings but lacks direct experimental validation. The suggestion is reasonable given the early STN dysfunction and its role in action suppression, but would require clinical or preclinical therapeutic studies to validate.

results.result: Background knowledge and context about basal ganglia circuitry, HD pathology, mouse models, NMDAR signaling, glutamate uptake, mitochondrial dysfunction, and KATP channels, drawn from the literature and used to frame the study.
results.evaluation: These claims (C60-C109 subset) represent established knowledge from the literature, appropriately cited and used to provide context for the study. They include information about basal ganglia function, HD genetics and symptoms, mouse model characteristics, and molecular mechanisms. While not novel findings, they are accurately represented and appropriately sourced. Some claims note controversies in the literature (e.g., C80-C81 regarding glutamate uptake), which is appropriate scholarly practice.
